hook.line: Promises usually come with a condition. "You can stay, as long as you pay your share." To make the condition, Spanish turns *mientras* into "as long as" with a small change in the verb.
hook.en: As long as there's work, I'm staying.

examples.en: As long as there's work, I'm staying.

examples.es: Puedes usar el carro mientras lo cuides.
examples.en: You can use the car as long as you look after it.
As long as it doesn't rain, we'll play.

examples.es: Mientras Tomás quiera, el café sigue abierto.
examples.en: As long as Tomás wants to, the café stays open.

examples.es: Mientras la fuente no hable, Mariana no puede publicar.
examples.en: As long as the source doesn't talk, Mariana can't publish.
While Vale cooks, Tomás serves the customers.

rule:
*Mientras* with the ordinary indicative means "while": two things happening together, *mientras Vale cocina, Tomás atiende*.

*Mientras* with the present subjunctive means "as long as": a condition for now or the future. *Mientras haya trabajo, me quedo*. The *-ar* verbs take *-e* (*cuides*), the *-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-a* (*haya*, *quiera*).

Never put a future after it: Spanish says *mientras haya*, not *mientras habrá*. The main clause can be present or future, as you like.
smallPrint: Teachers file this with the conditional connectors like *siempre que* and *con tal de que*. The subjunctive marks a condition, not a fact.

options: While you work, I study.
As long as you work, I study.
If you work, I study.
While you work, I study.
As long as you work, I'll study.
You worked while I studied.
As long as Vale cooks, Tomás serves.
While Vale cooks, Tomás serves.
Vale cooked while Tomás served.
While it isn't raining, we're playing.
It didn't rain, so we played.
As long as it doesn't rain, we'll play.
As long as there is work, I'm staying.
While there is work, I stayed.
There was work, so I stayed.

options: You can use the car while you look after it.
You can use the car as long as you look after it.
You used the car and looked after it.

While I talk, she listens.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right verb and type the whole sentence (as long as): *Mientras ___ trabajo, me quedo.* (*hay* or *haya*)
yourTurn.why: "As long as" is a condition, so the verb goes in the subjunctive: *haya*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right verb and type the whole sentence (while, at the same time): *Mientras Vale ___, Tomás atiende.* (*cocina* or *cocine*)
yourTurn.why: Two things happening together are facts, so the indicative *cocina* fits.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: As long as it doesn't rain, we'll play.
Type it in Spanish (to a friend): You can use the car as long as you look after it.
yourTurn.answer: Puedes usar el carro mientras lo cuides.
accept: Mientras lo cuides, puedes usar el carro.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: As long as Tomás wants to, the café stays open.
yourTurn.answer: Mientras Tomás quiera, el café sigue abierto.
accept: El café sigue abierto mientras Tomás quiera.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: As long as the source doesn't talk, Mariana can't publish.
yourTurn.answer: Mientras la fuente no hable, Mariana no puede publicar.
accept: Mariana no puede publicar mientras la fuente no hable.
yourTurn.why: *Hablar* is an *-ar* verb, so the subjunctive ends in *-e*: *hable*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change from while to as long as: *Mientras trabajas, yo estudio.* (you work)
yourTurn.why: Only the verb changes: *trabajas* becomes the subjunctive *trabajes*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. After *mientras* meaning "as long as", Spanish uses the present subjunctive, never the future.
With the indicative it would just mean "while there is work"; to set a condition you need *haya*.
To say "as long as it doesn't rain", use *no llueva*. The indicative *llueve* would mean "while it is raining".

personal: Make a promise to someone, with a condition, using *mientras* and the subjunctive: *Mientras…, yo…*.
